html:
In 1510 the Portuguese commander Afonso de Albuquerque captured Goa, a port on India's west coast, from the sultan of Bijapur. He took it in March, lost it, and took it back for good in November.

Albuquerque wanted a fixed base rather than a string of trading posts on rented land. Goa was an island town with a good harbour and a trade in Arabian and Persian war horses that the Deccan kingdoms needed. He made it the capital of the Estado da India, Portugal's empire of forts and sea lanes from Mozambique to Macau.

From Goa the Portuguese took Malacca in 1511 and Hormuz in 1515, and tried to force Asian ships to buy passes. Goa became a Catholic city with its own archbishop. Francis Xavier arrived in 1542, and the Inquisition followed in 1560. New plants from the Americas, among them chilli, entered India through its port.

Goa stayed Portuguese for 451 years, long after Portugal's other Indian holdings were gone, until India took it in 1961.
